questions.q: Why shouldn't a cloud credential ever be written into a .tfvars file that gets committed to Git?
options: Terraform treats .tfvars as plain text, so a committed credential sits in Git history forever, readable by anyone with repo access
Credentials placed in .tfvars are deleted automatically after the first terraform apply
.tfvars files are automatically encrypted by Git on commit
Terraform refuses to parse any .tfvars file that contains a secret value
questions.explain: A .tfvars file is just text, so a committed credential remains in Git history indefinitely, long after it might be rotated.

questions.q: How does the azurerm provider receive Service Principal credentials in the workflow example, without any Terraform code changing?
options: Terraform prompts interactively for credentials during terraform apply in CI
Through fixed environment variable names like ARM_CLIENT_ID and ARM_CLIENT_SECRET, supplied from GitHub Actions secrets
By reading a plaintext credentials.txt file checked into the repository
The provider has no way to accept credentials from environment variables
questions.explain: azurerm automatically reads ARM_CLIENT_ID, ARM_CLIENT_SECRET, ARM_TENANT_ID, and ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID from the environment if present, so the workflow just supplies them via secrets.

questions.q: What does adding `sensitive = true` to a Terraform output actually do?
options: Replaces the value with <sensitive> in all Terraform console output, including plan and apply
Removes the output from the configuration entirely
Prevents the resource from ever being created
Encrypts the value everywhere it is ever stored, including the state file
questions.explain: sensitive = true causes Terraform to print <sensitive> in place of the real value in plan and apply console output and logs.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does marking an output sensitive NOT protect against?
options: The resource being deleted during a future terraform destroy
The real value still being stored in plain text inside the Terraform state file
The value being visible to the Terraform CLI version number
The value appearing in the GitHub Actions workflow YAML file
questions.explain: Terraform still needs the real value in the state file to detect drift and plan correctly, so sensitive = true alone doesn't keep it out of state — a secured backend does that.

questions.q: Why does GitHub automatically mask the value of `secrets.ARM_CLIENT_SECRET` if it happens to appear in a workflow's log output?
options: GitHub does not mask secret values in logs under any circumstances
Because Terraform itself encrypts every line of its own log output
Because it's referenced through GitHub Actions' secrets store, which GitHub recognizes and redacts in logs
Because the value was declared with sensitive = true in an output block
questions.explain: Values pulled from the repository's configured GitHub Actions secrets are automatically masked by GitHub if they appear in log output, separate from Terraform's own sensitive output mechanism.
